budget_violations: High confidence (~85): Step 1 (lines 99-109) requires reading file contents that the stated retrieval budget never allocates. 'Take the Candidate list slot. If it resolves to a file, Glob for it and read the unit names' (line 101) — the Candidate list slot itself is defined as possibly '...a file that can be read' (line 48), so getting unit names out of it requires an actual Read (Glob only returns matching paths, it cannot return a file's contents). Two sentences later: 'Where a candidate is named by filelist rather than directory, expand it using the profile's Filelist convention' (lines 106-107) — expanding a filelist to resolve nested -f includes also requires reading its contents; Glob cannot parse a filelist body. Neither of these appears in the Read ledger, which states explicitly (lines 87-88): 'At most six windowed Read calls of about 60 lines, all in step 6, two apiece on the top three targets. Steps 4, 7, 8 and 9 open nothing.' By enumerating exactly which steps open nothing and allocating literally all Read budget to step 6, the retrieval budget implicitly asserts step 1 opens nothing either — which contradicts step 1's own instructions. The Grep ledger is fully spent elsewhere too (8 of 8: one in step 2, six in step 3, one in step 5), so there is no slack to reassign this as a Grep instead. Notably, 'read' in step 1 is the only tool-verb in the whole procedure that is NOT bolded (contrast **Glob**, **Grep**, **Read** bolded everywhere else including 6 times in step 6 alone) — evidence this was an oversight rather than a deliberate non-tool use of the word 'read'. This is carried out by a step that, per the review brief, 'cannot be carried out inside the skill's own caps' — a genuine hole in an otherwise unusually precise budget.

Lower confidence (~40): step 2, line 118, 'Note the port count from the header's neighbourhood without opening it' — for the case explicitly discussed two lines later ('A unit with four hundred ports'), seeing an accurate port count from Grep context alone (rather than a Read) is plausible only if the single module-header Grep call is run with enough trailing context lines to show the whole port list, which is never stated. Worth a one-line clarification but not clearly broken the way step 1 is.
review.open_twice: Yes, on balance — this reads like something a senior/staff formal engineer would keep bookmarked. The Gotchas section is genuinely dense with hard-won, technically correct specifics (cone-of-influence vs. total flop count, black-boxing as over-approximation vs. constraints as under-approximation, FIFO control-provable/data-not, the reset-to-ready latency subtraction on bounded proofs), the worst-blocker-not-average ranking logic is the right call for formal amenability, and the five-term effort decomposition with a mandatory abandon criterion directly targets the 'three-week proof nobody can cancel' failure mode named in the framing. The claim-type table (step 7) and the handoff to dv-formal-apps are honestly scoped. The one thing that would make a precise engineer stop trusting the file on a careful re-read is the step-1 budget contradiction (Read the candidate list / expand the filelist, with zero Read or Grep budget allocated to step 1) — this is exactly the kind of arithmetic a formal-planning audience checks, since the whole point of the skill is 'the budget accounts for every call it spends.' Fixing that one gap would make this a strong keeper; as shipped it would earn one skeptical flag on first read but the content underneath is worth returning to.

recheck.why: Lint is 1.000 and clean, check_pack returns 0 findings, the retrieval budget balances exactly (3 Glob / 8 Grep / 8 Read, every step accounted for), all 10 slots are spent, the handoff block obeys _shared/handoff-vocabulary.md (owner/evidence/notes shapes honoured, notes last, run id correctly refused, claim/blocker enums vs free-text siblings permitted by the registry's free-text rule), role/level are formal-verification/senior-staff, and the formal physics (bound minus reset-to-ready latency, FIFO depth floor, 2^W counter horizon, black-box over-approximation vs constraint under-approximation, uninterpreted datapath abstraction) is correct. But I would not hand it to a DV engineer today, for two independent reasons. First, the skill consumes a specification it never slots: budget rule 2 spends a Glob on "one spare for the specification directory in step 6" — a definite article for a house convention the author cannot know — and a failed guess drives blocker: spec-missing and then claim: not-a-target, the harshest verdict in the table; the nearest sibling dv-formal-property-authoring declares exactly this fact as a slot ("Spec extract"). Compounding it, step 4 says spec-missing is "Checked first as a gate" and the gotcha says it is "a gate before the ranking rather than a rank within it", yet nothing before step 6 looks for a spec and step 6 covers only "the top three targets", so candidates ranked 4..n structurally cannot receive the blocker that is supposed to precede ranking. Second, metric 6's black-box test is technically wrong: "any module name instantiated here that did not appear in step 2's headers ... is a black box", while step 2's Grep is "alternate the unit names in a single pattern" — candidates only. Every ordinary in-tree submodule of a candidate becomes a false black box, demoting clean control blocks from blocker: none to environment and writing an untrue black-box into abstraction/assumes; a black box is a module deliberately not analysed, not a child that happens to be off the candidate list. The stated noise for the same metric ("method and task calls share the shape") is also wrong — a bare task call is one identifier plus paren and obj.method( has no whitespace-separated second identifier — while assert property (, cover property (, function automatic bit foo( and module foo ( do match, and under the rule above they become black boxes named property or foo. A ranking skill whose ranking collapses this way is not shippable.

Add a slot in the pattern of dv-formal-property-authoring's 'Spec extract' (where this block's spec extract lives, and whether it is a file Read can open).

Ordering contradiction on the spec-missing gate: step 4 says 'Checked first as a gate' and the gotcha says 'a gate before the ranking rather than a rank within it', but the only step that looks for a spec is step 6, which is scoped to 'the top three targets'. Either make the gate reachable for every candidate from the new spec slot before step 4, or stop calling it a gate and say plainly it can only be assigned to the top three.

Step 3 metric 6: 'any module name instantiated here that did not appear in step 2's headers, or whose prefix appears in the Black-box policy slot, is a black box' is wrong, because step 2's Grep 'alternate[s] the unit names in a single pattern' and therefore only ever returns candidate headers. Every in-tree submodule of a candidate is falsely declared a black box, which pushes clean control blocks to blocker: environment and puts an untrue black-box into abstraction and assumes. Fix at no budget cost: anchor step 2's Grep on the module keyword plus any identifier across the RTL root, and still take each candidate's path and line from it.

Step 3 metric 6 'Known noise' is inaccurate and compounds the above: 'method and task calls share the shape' — a bare task call is one identifier plus an opening parenthesis, and obj.method( has no whitespace-separated second identifier. What actually matches 'identifier, instance name, opening parenthesis' is assert property (, cover property (, function automatic bit foo( and module foo (. Name those instead, or the false hits become false black boxes under the metric 6 comparison.
Human verification bullet 'nothing ranked blocker: none instantiates anything metric 6 could not resolve to a module header' repeats the same conflation and must be rewritten alongside metric 6.
new_problems: Metric 1's 'Known noise' is factually wrong: 'packed multi-dimensional vectors match and are not memories' — a packed multi-dimensional declaration is logic [3:0][7:0] x; with adjacent brackets and no identifier between them, so it cannot match a pattern requiring 'closing bracket, identifier, opening bracket'. The noise that does match is an unpacked array of nets used as a per-port bus array in generate code, and typedef'd array types; neither is named.

Metric 6's noise column names a case that cannot match (method and task calls) and omits the ones that do (assert property (, cover property (, function/task declarations with a return type, module headers).
